findings.statement: CXCL8 is the best literature-supported node of the axis formed by CXCL8 with its receptors CXCR1 and CXCR2: PMID:33706134 states the axis participates in UC pathogenesis via PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signalling. Mucosal meta-analysis log2FC is [gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.704]. These are bioinformatic or mechanistic studies, not clinical trials in UC.

CXCR2 ranks first in convergence (expression, replication, genetics and clinical-stage antagonists in Open Targets) but has no extracted literature relations in this corpus. Only passing mentions exist: CXCR2 is listed among hub genes of active UC (PMID:38448514). No UC clinical evidence for antagonists of CXCR1 or CXCR2 was found in the corpus.

CXCL8 diagnostic value is modest and from a blood RNA-seq validation set in IBD (not UC-specific): in PMID:40622593 CXCL8 had lower diagnostic performance than ITGA5. It was also a PPI hub gene in PMID:35719390, and PXR is proposed to inhibit CXCL8 expression (PMID:33686088, speculative).

IDO1 has direct mechanistic evidence in one study (PMID:40370742): expression is elevated in UC patients and correlates with M1 macrophage polarization, IDO1 induces M1 polarization via the ER stress GRP78-XBP1 pathway, and a methyl-tryptophan IDO inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis. Mucosal meta-analysis log2FC is [gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.445]. Evidence is a single group, in mice plus human data; it is expression-driven with no genetic support.

CHI3L1 is upregulated in UC and correlates with NLRP3 inflammasome expression; PMID:41314595 reports it promotes macrophage pyroptosis through BCAT1/NF-kappaB, and exogenous NF-kappaB activation reversed the protective effect of CHI3L1 inhibition. Velpatasvir binding to recombinant CHI3L1 was shown by microscale thermophoresis (PMID:42508656), a repurposing lead only. Mucosal meta-analysis log2FC is [gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.714]. The macrophage-centred mechanism suggests the signal partly reflects infiltrating immune cells.

DUOX2 is among the most elevated proteins in inflamed UC biopsies versus healthy controls (PMID:39280905), is shared by IBD and CRC signatures (PMID:35432477), and is proposed as a credible diagnostic biomarker (PMID:38070204). A herbal formula (TLXDS) is reported to alleviate UC by inhibiting DUOX2 overexpression, with the authors saying DUOX2 may serve as a key therapeutic target (PMID:42974467). Evidence is mostly correlative or herbal-pharmacology based; no DUOX2-specific drug exists.

MMP1 tracks treatment: mirikizumab-modified transcripts correlating with modified Mayo, Geboes and Robarts indices include MMP1, MMP3, S100A8 and IL1B (PMID:36881820). A separate study reports strong diagnostic potential for MMP1 and ilomastat as a docking-predicted inhibitor (PMID:40681672); the MMP1 diagnostic claim there concerns UC-associated CRC. CD274, MMP1, NCF2 and PLAU were positively associated with macrophage infiltration (PMID:41368353). Mostly bioinformatic.

AQP9 is predominantly expressed in neutrophils and upregulated in UC mouse colon; PMID:41504039 reports it promotes NET formation via JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis, aggravating epithelial injury. Because the signal is neutrophil-restricted, its tissue-level upregulation reflects neutrophil infiltration rather than epithelial change. No drug targets AQP9 and the evidence is preclinical.

SLC26A2, downregulated in the ranking, is reported down in the mucosa of active UC versus healthy controls, with lower levels diagnostic and correlated with Mayo score and PUCAI; it correlates positively with CLDN3 and negatively with IL-17A (PMID:40002875). Single study; the epithelial-loss direction is the only down-regulated epithelial candidate with direct UC literature in this set.

S100A9 is reported to perform excellently for diagnosing active UC (PMID:38448514), is up in UC by ONT-RNA-seq (PMID:39955510), and in tofacitinib-treated patients S100A9 is downregulated in resident macrophages with response (PMID:40320713). It is a neutrophil/myeloid-derived marker; no direct S100A9 drug in Open Targets.

LCN2 is higher in short-duration UC than long-duration UC, and both exceed UC-associated cancer and normal tissue (PMID:35111677), proposed as a marker for UC-associated carcinogenesis related to disease duration. This indicates its level falls with progression to cancer, so diagnostic value depends on context.

CXCL1 is repeatedly proposed as a diagnostic marker (PMID:38070204, PMID:40791849, PMID:37495756), but its individual performance is modest: in PMID:37495756 it was a weaker activity marker than CYP2R1, NEU4 and LPCAT1. All support is bioinformatic signature work.

CD274 (PD-L1), a top-ranked gene with expression and Open Targets support, has no extracted literature relations in this corpus; its only UC mention is as a bioinformatic macrophage-infiltration hub gene (cited under MMP1). No UC therapeutic evidence; checkpoint agonism rather than blockade would be the relevant direction, and this is not addressed in the corpus.

OSMR has no literature relations in the graph, though a mirikizumab study (PMID:36881820) lists OSMR with IL-1B, FCGR3A/B and CXCL6 as transcripts associated with resistance to current therapies, suggesting anti-IL23p19 modulates pathways of anti-TNF and JAK inhibitor resistance. Genetic and tractability support (vixarelimab) is thus not matched by direct UC literature.

caveats: Literature relations are LLM-extracted from a small abstract corpus (about 300 abstracts); counts are not a measure of clinical importance.
CXCR1, CXCR2, CD274, JAK2, IL2RA, FCGR2A, OSMR, PI3, CXCL5, REG1A, DUOXA2 and CDH3 have strong expression/Open Targets support but zero or near-zero extracted literature relations.
Most biomarker claims come from bioinformatic hub-gene or ML signatures with limited external validation; AUC values were not annotated numerically.
The tofacitinib corpus study (PMID:40320713) reports about two-fifths response and links non-response to macrophage activation, but it does not directly implicate JAK2 as a gene-level target.
Several genes (AQP9, S100A8/9, LCN2, CXCL8) are neutrophil/myeloid markers, so tissue upregulation may reflect infiltration, not epithelial change.
